activities.title: Say words with two consonants side by side
materials: list: stop, flag, swim, grab, plan, frog, step, clap
parentPrompts: Keep small items like buttons, coins, and seeds out of mouths, and stay close while your child plays.
Explain: "In a blend, two letters stand side by side and you hear both sounds quickly, like s-t in stop." Say "stop" slowly: s-t-o-p.
Use sound boxes with four boxes. Say a word from your list and have your child push one counter per sound. Ask: "How many sounds? Which two sounds are right next to each other?"
Play "chop the word": you say the sounds slowly (f-r-o-g), and your child blends them into the word.
Reverse it: you say the word, and your child chops it into sounds on their fingers.
Check: your child can say all four sounds in at least five of the eight words and can blend a word you chop.

activities.title: Build words that start with two consonants
materials: blend cards: st, fl, pl, cl, sl, dr, tr
ending cards: op, ap, ip, ug
parentPrompts: Make the blend cards in one color and the ending cards in another. Put st + op together and read "stop." Slide the cards apart and read each part.
Make new words by swapping the blend: stop, flop, plop, drop. Ask: "Is it a real word? What does it mean?"
Do the same with ap, ip, and ug (clap, flap, slap, trip, drip, clip, plug, slug).
Have your child write three of the words on paper and read them back to you.
Check: your child reads the blend as two quick sounds (not guessing) in at least eight of the words.

subject: literacy
title: Ending blends: nd, st, mp, nk

activities.title: Read and write words that end in two consonants
materials: list: hand, sand, nest, best, jump, lamp, camp, sink, pink
parentPrompts: Write "hand" on a card. Say it slowly and tap each sound: h-a-n-d. Ask: "What two sounds are at the end?"
Read the list together, tapping a finger for each sound. Sort the cards by ending: nd, st, mp, nk.
Dictate three words (sand, jump, pink). Have your child say the sounds slowly and write the letters they hear.
Say a silly sentence for your child to finish aloud: "I will jump on the ___." Let them choose a word from the cards.
Check: they can read the words and write the ending blend correctly for at least two of the three dictated words.

activities.title: Retell a picture book in order
materials: a picture book with a clear story (any from your shelf or library)
parentPrompts: Read the book aloud once. Stop now and then to ask: "What do you think happens next?" Keep it light.
Ask: "Who is in the story? Where does it happen?" Then label the three paper sections Beginning, Middle, End.
Have your child draw one important moment in each section while telling you what happened. Write a short caption they dictate.
Ask: "What did the character learn or what was the big idea?" Accept any answer your child can support from the book.
Check: your child tells the three parts in order, naming at least one character and the setting, using key details from the book.

activities.title: Write words by stretching the sounds
materials: a few small toys or pictures (a frog, a clip, a drum, a plug)
parentPrompts: Put three toys on the table. Pick one and say its name slowly. Ask: "What do you hear first? Next?"
Have your child write the word using the sounds they hear. Invented spelling is fine, such as "frg" for frog. Do not correct right away.
Write the word the standard way underneath and compare: "You heard every sound. This word also needs an o in the middle." Praise what is right.
Do three or four more words. Then read all of them together.
Check: most of the sounds in each word appear in your child's spelling, in the right order.

activities.title: Learn doubles and one more
materials: a mirror or a drawing of two matching hands
parentPrompts: Show doubles with a picture: two hands with 3 fingers each is 3 + 3 = 6. Build doubles to 5 + 5 with counters and say them aloud.
Make a doubles poster: 1 + 1, 2 + 2, up to 5 + 5, with a small drawing for each.
Introduce "doubles plus one": 4 + 5 is 4 + 4 and one more, so 9. Try 3 + 4 and 5 + 6.
Roll a die, then roll it again. If the numbers match, shout "Double!" Add each pair of rolls.
Check: your child answers doubles to 5 + 5 without counting and uses doubles to solve one near-double.

activities.title: Build fact family houses
materials: three numbers per family, such as 2, 5, 7; 3, 4, 7; 4, 6, 10
parentPrompts: Draw a roof (triangle) with three numbers: 2, 5, 7. Write the facts: 2 + 5 = 7, 5 + 2 = 7, 7 - 2 = 5, 7 - 5 = 2.
Show with counters that 2 + 5 and 5 + 2 give the same total. Ask: "Does the order change the answer?" (It does not for addition.)
Pick a second family, such as 3, 4, 7. Have your child write all four facts. Then a third family with a total of 10.
Play "which fact does not belong?" Write three correct facts from one family and one wrong one. Ask your child to find it.
Check: your child writes all four facts for one family and explains that you can add in either order.

activities.title: Balance equations
materials: a ruler or pencil balanced on a roll of tape, or a homemade balance (a ruler over a book)
parentPrompts: Show a balanced seesaw. Say: "The equal sign means both sides have the same amount." Put 3 counters on one side and 2 + 1 on the other.
Write 3 = 2 + 1. Ask: "Does it still balance?" Write other forms, like 5 = 5, 4 + 1 = 3 + 2.
Play true or false. Say each equation aloud and show it: 6 = 4 + 2 (true), 7 = 5 + 1 (false), 3 + 3 = 2 + 4 (true), 8 - 2 = 5 (false).
Ask your child to make up one true equation and one false equation.
Check: your child correctly decides true or false for at least three of four equations and explains in a sentence what = means.

activities.title: Solve for the missing number
parentPrompts: Write 5 + __ = 9. Ask: "What number goes in the blank?" Show it with counters: five on the table, nine in all, find how many to add.
Hide counters under a cup to show it. Count on from 5 to 9 on fingers: six, seven, eight, nine, that is four more.
Try 3 + __ = 7, __ + 2 = 6, 8 - __ = 3. Let your child draw or use counters.
Make a mystery number puzzle for each other. The unknown can be anywhere.
Check: your child finds the missing number for at least three problems and can show how they know.

activities.title: Count up to find the difference
materials: a number line to 20 on paper
parentPrompts: Ask: "I have 8 stickers and I want 10. How many more do I need?" Count up from 8 to 10 on the number line: nine, ten, two more.
Connect: "10 - 8 is 2 because 8 + 2 is 10." Say the pair of facts together.
Try 9 - 6, 7 - 4, and 10 - 3. For each, put the token on the smaller number and hop up to the larger one.
Ask: "Is it faster to count back or count up for 10 - 8? What about 10 - 3?" There is no one right answer; let your child explain.
Check: your child solves three subtraction problems by counting up and writes the matching addition fact.

activities.title: Find roots, stem, leaves
materials: a small potted plant or a plant outside (a weed pulled with its roots is fine)
parentPrompts: Keep small items like buttons, coins, and seeds out of mouths, and stay close while your child plays.
Look closely at the plant with your child. Find the leaves, the stem, and the roots (if you have a pulled plant). Ask: "What does each part look like?"
Explain: roots hold the plant in place and take in water from the soil; the stem holds the plant up and carries water to the leaves; leaves use sunlight to help the plant make its food.
Draw the plant and label root, stem, and leaf. Add a flower if it has one; many plants make flowers that later grow seeds.
Play "what part am I?": "I hold the plant in the ground" (roots), "I hold the leaves up" (stem).
Check: your child can name three parts of a plant and say one job for each. Safety: wash hands after touching soil and plants; do not eat any plant unless you know it is safe.

activities.title: Start a bean seed
parentPrompts: Fold a damp (not dripping) paper towel and place it in the bag. Add the beans so they are visible through the bag.
Ask: "What do you think will happen? What does a seed need?" Write your child's prediction. Tape the bag in a sunny window.
Draw the seed on day one. Check it every day or two for a week and draw what changes. Many beans show roots in 3 to 7 days.
Talk about what comes out first: a root, then a stem and leaves.

Check: your child makes a prediction, draws at least two days of observation, and says one thing seeds need to start growing (water). Safety: keep the dry beans away from mouths, since they are a choking hazard; throw out the bag if you see mold.

activities.title: Plants in different conditions
materials: 3 small cups with soil and a few quick-growing seeds (such as grass or bean seeds), or 3 similar plants
a dark place such as a closet
parentPrompts: Plant seeds in three cups of soil (or use three similar plants). Label them: sun and water; sun, no water; no light, with water.
Ask: "Which plant do you think will grow best? Why?" Record your child's idea.
Check them every day for a week. Water them only as planned. Draw what you notice.
At the end, compare. Ask: "What did the plants need?" (Light and water help most plants grow.)
Check: your child says what each plant needed and what happened when it was missing. Safety: wash hands; keep soil away from mouths.

activities.title: Walk and spot safety signs
materials: a clipboard or a book to write on
a walk outside or picture of streets
parentPrompts: Take a short walk or look at pictures. Find signs: stop signs, crosswalk signs, and traffic lights. Ask: "What does each one tell us?"
Talk about why we cross at crosswalks, hold an adult's hand, and look both ways. Practice at a safe crossing with an adult.
Draw three signs and write what each means.
Play "red light, green light" at home as a game and talk about why the real lights matter.
Check: your child explains what two signs mean and why they help people stay safe. Safety: stay with your child near any road.

activities.title: Write a family agreement
materials: a time when the whole family can talk
parentPrompts: Ask each person: "What helps our home run well?" Write down ideas.
Choose three or four rules everyone agrees on. Use positive words: "We talk kindly."
Decorate the poster. Everyone who lives in your home can sign or draw a handprint.
Talk about what to do when someone forgets a rule: "What is a kind reminder?"
Check: your child names the rules and says one reason for each. Hang it where everyone can see it.
